title: Be Present They Said
author: Rich Carr
summary: Rich Carr argues that the executive presence and mindfulness industry has built a profitable apparatus on top of the floor of presence -- but presence is only the floor, not the house. He opens with two cases where being perfectly calm and 'present' still produced failed conversations: a CFO meeting where the leader missed that her counterpart was upset before he even sat down, and a Chevron pitch where he never registered that the senior buyer had been dragged in against his will. Carr traces how Goleman, Brown, and Nouwen all identified the missing cognitive pieces (cognitive empathy, perspective-taking, interior stability) but the industry downstream of them flattened everything into 'be warmer' and sold a feeling. His prescription is the 'AIR' framework: Catch (notice what the other person is carrying before they speak), Read (interpret what it means), Act (prove you read it correctly by what you do next). Presence gets you to the door; this is what happens after you walk through it.
points: Presence is real and necessary but it is only the floor -- the person who wins the hard conversation is not the most present but the one who knows what to do with their presence once they have it.

The industry sold a state of being (calmness, groundedness, eye contact) when what leaders actually needed was a skill: the ability to catch what the other person is carrying into the room before they say a word.

Goleman, Brown, and Nouwen all named the missing cognitive pieces -- cognitive empathy, perspective-taking, interior stability -- but the industry downstream flattened all three into 'be warmer' and sold the feeling, not the skill.

The 'AIR' framework -- Catch, Read, Act -- makes explicit the three moves that distinguish a leader who uses presence effectively from one who is merely calm and completely blind to what is happening in the room.

Executive presence programs and weekend retreats develop better posture, breath, and eye contact while leaving leaders with the exact same inability to read what the person across the table actually walked in carrying.
quotes: She came home Monday grounded, centered, ready to lead. Tuesday she sat down with her CFO. Present, breathing, fully in her body. Ninety seconds in, the conversation slid sideways and stayed there.

The CFO walked in carrying something, the way everybody does. Maybe the budget numbers came in ugly that morning. Maybe his kid announced she's dropping out of college. Whatever it was, it was written all over him before he pulled out his chair.

Two days later I walk into the Chevron conference room breathing from my diaphragm, slowed way down, fully present, and I watch the senior buyer fold his arms inside ninety seconds. Because I never registered, in all that lovely presence, that the man had been dragged into the meeting against his will and hated every minute of it.
Don't get me wrong. Presence is real, and it matters. It's the floor. Table stakes. Without it you're too far inside your own head to perceive the room at all. But the floor isn't the house.

Daniel Goleman, who gets cited constantly, breaks empathy into three things, and one of them is cognitive empathy, an actual thinking move. The training industry flattened all three into 'be warmer.' Goleman was pointing at a skill, and warmth was just the easiest part to sell.
Brene Brown's empathy video has tens of millions of views, says plainly that empathy takes perspective-taking. That's a cognitive act. People quote her and sell the feeling. She named the thinking.

So next time somebody tells you the fix for your communication problems is to 'be more present,' ask them what you're supposed to do with the presence once you have it. Watch them stall. That stall is the whole game made visible.
